questions.stem:
Figure 1 shows how 25 people travelled to work.

Their travel to work is represented by the events

$B$ bicycle

$T$ train

$W$ walk

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Write down 2 of these events that are mutually exclusive. Give a reason for your answer.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: $B, W$ or $T, W$ [accept $B \cup T, W$ or $B \cap T, W$] (condone $\mathrm{P}(B)$, $\mathrm{P}(W)$ etc)
B1: Since there is no overlap between the events (o.e.) (accept comment in context e.g. "no one walks and takes the train")
Official notes (completeness pass):
- 1st B1 for a suitable pair. Do not accept universally exclusive pairs such as $B$ and $B'$ etc
- 2nd B1 for any correct statement. Accept use of symbols e.g.: $B\cap W=\varnothing$ or $\mathrm{P}(T\cap W)=0$ etc But $T\cap W=0$ is B0 (since it is not a correct statement)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Determine whether or not $B$ and $T$ are independent events.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: e.g. $\mathrm{P}(B) = \frac{9}{25}$, $\mathrm{P}(T) = \frac{8}{25}$, $\mathrm{P}(B \cap T) = \frac{5}{25}$
M1: $\mathrm{P}(B \cap T) \neq \mathrm{P}(B) \times \mathrm{P}(T)$ [$0.2 \neq 0.36 \times 0.32 = 0.1152$ o.e.]
A1cso: So $B$ and $T$ are not independent
Official notes (completeness pass):
- 1st M1 for an attempt at all required probabilities with labels for a suitable test (allow one error). Accept use of A and B as long as they can be identified as B and T by correct probabilities. Must be probabilities not integers such as 5, 9, 8 etc for both these M marks
- 2nd M1 for $\mathrm{P}(B)\times\mathrm{P}(T)$ evaluated (correct for their probabilities) or $\mathrm{P}(B\cap T)\neq\mathrm{P}(B)\times\mathrm{P}(T)$ stated or implied in symbols or using their probabilities. or $\mathrm{P}(B|T)\neq\mathrm{P}(B)$ or $\mathrm{P}(T|B)\neq\mathrm{P}(T)$ stated or implied in symbols or using their probabilities.
- A1 for a conclusion of not independent. Requires all probabilities used to be correct and seen. This A mark is dependent on both Ms
- NB $\mathrm{P}(B|T)=\frac{5}{8}$ & $\mathrm{P}(B)=\frac{9}{25}$ or $\mathrm{P}(T|B)=\frac{5}{9}$ & $\mathrm{P}(T)=\frac{8}{25}$ seen, followed by a correct conclusion scores 3/3

parts.label: c
parts.text:
One person is chosen at random.

Find the probability that this person

(c) walks to work,
(1)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) travels to work by bicycle and train.
(1)

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) Given that this person travels to work by bicycle, find the probability that they will also take the train.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) M1: $[\mathrm{P}(T|B)=] \frac{\mathrm{P}(T \cap B)}{\mathrm{P}(B)} = \frac{\text{"(d)"}}{(5+4)/25}$
A1: $= \frac{5}{9}$ or $0.\dot{5}$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for a correct ratio of probabilities e.g. $\frac{5/25}{(5+4)/25}$ or $\frac{5}{5+4}$ or A correct ratio expression and at least one correct (or correct f.t.) probability substituted.
- A1 for $\frac{5}{9}$ with no incorrect working seen but $\frac{5}{9}$ following from $\mathrm{P}(B|T)$ is 0/2. $\frac{5}{9}$ alone is 2/2

questions.stem: A policeman records the speed of the traffic on a busy road with a 30 mph speed limit. He records the speeds of a sample of 450 cars. The histogram in Figure 2 represents the results.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Calculate the number of cars that were exceeding the speed limit by at least 5 mph in the sample.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: One large square $= \frac{450}{\text{"22.5"}}$ or one small square $= \frac{450}{\text{"562.5"}}$ (o.e. e.g. $\frac{\text{"562.5"}}{450}$)
A1: One large square $= 20$ cars or one small square $= 0.8$ cars or 1 car $=1.25$ squares
dM1: No. $>35$ mph is: $4.5 \times \text{"20"}$ or $112.5 \times \text{"0.8"}$ (or equivalent e.g. using fd)
A1: $=90$ (cars)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- 1st M1 for attempt to count squares (accept "22.5" in [22, 23] and "562.5" in [550, 575]) and use 450 to obtain a measure of scale. [If using fd must use 450 to obtain scale factor]
- 1st A1 for a correct calc. for 20 or 0.8 or 1.25 etc [May be fd = 4 to 1 large sq. or 0.8 to 1 small sq. May be on the diagram.]
- 2nd dM1 dep on 1st M1 for correctly counting squares for > 35 mph and forming suitable expr'. 2nd A1 for 90 with no incorrect working seen.
- e.g. $\frac{4.5}{22.5}\times450$ scores M1A1M1 and A1 when = 90 is seen. Answer only is 4/4

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Estimate the value of the mean speed of the cars in the sample.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: $[\bar{x}=] \frac{30\times12.5+240\times25+90\times32.5+30\times37.5+60\times42.5}{450}$
M1: $\left[=\frac{12975}{450}\right]$
A1: $=28.83...$ or $\frac{173}{6}$ awrt $28.8$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- 1st M1 for clear, sensible use of mid-points at least 3 of (12.5, 25, 32.5, 37.5, 42.5) seen. 2nd M1 for an expression for $\bar{x}$ (at least 3 correct terms on num' and a compatible denominator) Follow through their frequencies.
- You may see these fractions: $\frac{16218.75}{562.5}$ (small squares), $\frac{12975}{450}$ (frequencies), $\frac{648.75}{22.5}$ (large squares). A1 for awrt 28.8 (answer only is 3/3)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Estimate, to 1 decimal place, the value of the median speed of the cars in the sample.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: $[Q_2=] 20+\frac{195}{240}\times 10$ (o.e.) [Allow use of $(n+1)$ giving 195.5 instead of 195]
A1: $=28.125$ [Use of $(n+1)$ gives $28.145...$] awrt $28.1$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for a full expression for median (using their frequencies). May see e.g. $25+\frac{75}{120}\times5$ etc. Do nor accept boundaries of 19.5 or 20.5, these are M0A0
- A1 for awrt 28.1 (answer only is 2/2) [For use of (n + 1) accept 28.15 but not 28.2]

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Comment on the shape of the distribution. Give a reason for your answer.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) B1ft: $Q_2 < \bar{x}$ [Condone $Q_2 \approx \bar{x}$]
dB1ft: So positive skew [so (almost) symmetric]
Official notes (completeness pass):
- 1st B1ft for a correct statement about their $Q_2$ and $\bar{x}$ [Condone $Q_2\approx\bar{x}$ only if $|Q_2-\bar{x}|<1$] Do not accept an argument based on the shape of the graph alone.
- 2nd dB1ft dependent on 1st B1 for a compatible description of skewness. F.t. their values
- Quartiles: If $Q_1=23.4$ and $Q_3=33.7\sim33.8$ are seen allow comparison of quartiles for 1st B1 in (d)

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) State, with a reason, whether the estimate of the mean or the median is a better representation of the average speed of the traffic on the road.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) [If chose skew in (d)] B1: median ($Q_2$); dB1: Since the data is skewed or median not affected by extreme values
[If chose symmetric in (d)] B1: mean ($\bar{x}$); dB1: Since it uses all the data
Official notes (completeness pass):
- 1st B1 for a correct choice based on their skewness comment in (d). If no choice made in (d) only $Q_2$. 2nd dB1 for a suitable compatible comment

questions.stem: The heights of an adult female population are normally distributed with mean 162 cm and standard deviation 7.5 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen adult female is taller than 150 cm.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: $[z=]\pm\left(\frac{150-162}{7.5}\right)$
A1: $[z=]-1.6$
A1: $[\mathrm{P}(F>150)=\mathrm{P}(Z>-1.6)=]$ awrt $0.945$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for attempting to standardise with 150, 162 and 7.5. Accept $\pm$. Allow use of symmetry and therefore 174 instead of 150
- 1st A1 for $-1.6$ seen. Allow 1.6 seen if 174 used or awrt 0.945 is seen. Sight of 0.945(2) is A1.
- 2nd A1 for awrt 0.945 Do not apply ISW, if 0.9452 is followed by 1 – 0.9452 then award A0. Correct answer only 3/3

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Sarah is a young girl. She visits her doctor and is told that she is at the 60th percentile for height.

(b) Assuming that Sarah remains at the 60th percentile, estimate her height as an adult.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) B1: $z=\pm 0.2533$ (or better seen)
M1: $(\pm)\frac{s-162}{7.5}=0.2533(47...)$
A1: $s=163.9$ awrt $164$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1 for $(z=)\pm0.2533$ (or better) seen. Giving $z=\pm0.25$ or $\pm0.253$ scores B0 here but may get M1A1
- M1 for standardising with s (o.e.), 162 and 7.5, allow $\pm$, and setting equal to a z value. Only allow $0.24\le z\le0.26$ Condone e.g. 160 for 162 etc
- A1 for awrt 164 (Correct answer only scores B0M1A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The heights of an adult male population are normally distributed with standard deviation 9.0 cm.

Given that 90% of adult males are taller than the mean height of adult females,

(c) find the mean height of an adult male.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) B1: $z=\pm 1.2816$ (or better seen)
M1: $\frac{162-\mu}{9}=-1.2815515...$
A1: correct equation with compatible signs and $1.26<|z|<1.31$
A1: $\mu=173.533...$ awrt $174$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1 for $(z=)\pm1.2816$ (or better) seen. Allow awrt $\pm1.28$ if B0 scored in (b) for z = awrt$\pm$0.25
- M1 for attempting to standardise with 162, 9 and $\mu$, and setting equal to a z value where $1.26<|z|<1.31$. Allow $\pm$ here so signs don't have to be compatible.
- 2nd A1 for awrt 174 (Correct answer only scores B0M1A1A1). Dependent on 1st A1
- An equation $\frac{162-\mu}{9}=1.2816$ leading to an answer of $\mu=174$ is A0A0 unless there is clear correct working such as: $\frac{162-x}{9}=1.2816\Rightarrow x=\ldots\therefore\mu=162+(162-x)=174$ then award A1A1
- NB A common error is: $\frac{162-\mu}{9}=1.2816$ followed by $\mu=162+9\times1.2816$ = awrt 174 It gets A0A0

questions.stem: A manufacturer carried out a survey of the defects in their soft toys. It is found that the probability of a toy having poor stitching is 0.03 and that a toy with poor stitching has a probability of 0.7 of splitting open. A toy without poor stitching has a probability of 0.02 of splitting open.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Draw a tree diagram to represent this information.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: 2 branch then 4 branch shape
dB1: labels showing stitching (accept letters) and 0.03 value correctly placed
dB1: labels showing splitting and 0.7 and 0.02 correctly placed
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Allow MR of 0.2 for 0.02 or 0.3 for 0.03 on tree diagram to score all M and A1ft marks only
- [probabilities shown in brackets are not required and any such values given can be ignored in (a)]

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen soft toy has exactly one of the two defects, poor stitching or splitting open.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: $\mathrm{P}(\text{Exactly one defect}) = 0.03\times0.3+0.97\times0.02$ or $\mathrm{P}(PS\cup Split)-2\mathrm{P}(PS\cap Split)$
A1ft: fully correct expression
A1cao: $=[0.009+0.0194=]0.0284$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for $0.03\times p+0.02\times q$ where p and q follow from their tree diagram. Extra terms is M0
- 1st A1ft for a fully correct expression. Accept $1-0.7$ for 0.3 and $1-0.03$ for 0.97 Follow through 0.2 and 0.3 MR only
- MR 0.2 for 0.02 $\to$ 0.203 or 0.3 for 0.03 $\to$ 0.104 or both $\to$ 0.23 should score M1A1A0
- 2nd A1 cao for 0.0284 only (or exact equivalent such as $\frac{71}{2500}$)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The manufacturer also finds that soft toys can become faded with probability 0.05 and that this defect is independent of poor stitching or splitting open. A soft toy is chosen at random.

(c) Find the probability that the soft toy has none of these 3 defects.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: $\mathrm{P}(\text{No defects}) = (1-0.03)(1-0.02)(1-0.05)$ (or better)
A1cao: $=$ awrt $0.903$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Do not allow 0.5 as MR of 0.05 so no M or A marks in (c) or (d)
- M1 for (their 0.97)$\times$(their 0.98)$\times(1-0.05)$ (or better) f.t. values from their tree diagram

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Find the probability that the soft toy has exactly one of these 3 defects.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: one correct triple (or correct ft from their tree) of: $[0.03\times0.3\times(1-0.05)]+[0.97\times0.02\times(1-0.05)]+[0.97\times0.98\times0.05]$
M1: two correct triples or correct ft from their tree and adding or their (b)$\times(1-0.05)$
A1ft: fully correct expression or ft their (b) and 0.2 or 0.3 MR only
A1cao: $=[0.02698+0.04753=]0.07451$ awrt $0.0745$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- P(Exactly one defect) = (b)$\times(1-0.05)$ + $(1-0.03)\times(1-0.02)\times0.05$ = "0.0284"$\times0.95+0.97\times0.98\times0.05$
- MR 0.2 for 0.02 $\to$ 0.23165 or 0.3 for 0.03 $\to$ 0.1331 or both $\to$ 0.2465 (or awrt 3sf) scores M1M1A1A0
